Will you?”

His eyes brightened, and he says:

“I'll help you steal him!”

Well, I lost my grip on everything then, just as if somebody'd shot me. I never heard such an astonishing thing—and I have to say Tom Sawyer sank a good deal in my opinion. Still, I couldn't believe it. Tom Sawyer stealing a nigger!

“Oh, shucks!” I says. “You're only fooling.”

“I ain't fooling at all.”

“Well, then,” says I, “whether you're fooling or not, if anybody says anything about a runaway nigger, mind you remember that you don't know a thing about him, and neither do I.”

We lifted the trunk into my wagon then, and he went his way and I went mine. Of course, being so glad and having so much to think about, I clean forgot to drive slowly; so I arrived home a mighty sight too soon for such a journey. The old gentleman stood in the doorway, and says:

“Well, that's wonderful! Who'd ever have guessed the mare had it in her? I wish we'd took her time. And not a hair on her is sweaty—not one. Wonderful! Why, I wouldn't sell that horse for a hundred dollars now; honest, I wouldn't. Before this I'd have let her go for fifteen and reckoned I'd got all she was worth.”

He didn't say anything else. He was the best, most innocent old soul I ever met. But that warn't so strange, because he wasn't merely a farmer; he preached, too. He had a little one-horse log church behind the plantation, built with his own hands and paid for himself, to serve for a church and schoolhouse. He never charged a cent for preaching, and it was worth every bit of that. There was lots of other farmer-preachers down South who carried on the same way.

Half an hour or thereabouts later, Tom's wagon came up to the front stile. Aunt Sally spotted it through the window, for it wasn't more than fifty yards off, and says:

“Why, somebody's arrived! Whoever can it be? Why, I declare I think it's a stranger. Jimmy”—he's one of the children—“run tell Lize to set another plate for dinner.”

Everybody hurried to the front door, because a stranger doesn't turn up every year, naturally, and when one does he's more interesting than the yaller-fever. Tom had crossed the stile and was coming towards the house; the wagon was rolling away along the village road, and all of us were crowded in the doorway. Tom was wearing his store clothes and had himself an audience—and that always suited Tom Sawyer down to the ground.

And I call on you, spirits of the dead, and on you, wandering spirits of revenge, to help me and guide my work. Let the cursed, hellish monster suffer deeply. Let him feel the despair that torments me now.”

I had begun this appeal solemnly, filled with an awe that almost convinced me the spirits of my murdered friends heard and approved my promise. But as I reached the end, a terrible fury took hold of me, and anger choked my voice.

A loud, devilish laugh answered me through the quiet night. It rang painfully in my ears for a long time, echoing from the mountains, until I felt that all of hell surrounded me with mocking laughter. Surely I would have gone mad at that moment and ended my miserable life, if my vow had not been heard and my life preserved for revenge. As the laughter faded, a familiar, hated voice seemed to whisper clearly beside my ear: “I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have decided to live, and I am satisfied.”

I rushed towards the place the sound had come from, but the devil escaped my grasp. Suddenly the broad moon rose, shining directly on his dreadful, twisted figure as he fled faster than any human could run.

I followed him, and for many months that has been my only task. With a faint clue to guide me, I traced the winding course of the Rhone, but without success. I reached the blue Mediterranean, where a strange chance allowed me to see the fiend board a ship at night and hide himself aboard. It was sailing for the Black Sea. I booked passage on the same vessel, but somehow he escaped. I do not know how.

Through the wild regions of Tartary and Russia I have continued following his trail, though he still avoids me. Sometimes peasants, frightened by the horrible sight of him, told me which way he had gone. Sometimes he left a sign himself to direct me, fearing that if I lost his trail completely I would give up hope and die. Snow fell on my head, and on the white plain I saw the marks of his enormous feet. You are only beginning your life; worry is new to you, and you have never known agony. How can you understand what I have felt and still feel? Cold, hunger, and exhaustion were the least of my destined sufferings. Some devil had cursed me, and I carried my everlasting hell wherever I went. Yet a good spirit still followed and guided my steps. When I complained most bitterly, it suddenly rescued me from difficulties that had seemed impossible to overcome. Sometimes, when hunger and exhaustion had nearly defeated my body, a meal awaited me in the wilderness and restored my strength and courage.

Are you talking about—Mr. Knightley?”

“Of course I am. I could never have meant anyone else, and I thought you understood. When we spoke about him, it seemed perfectly clear.”

“Not entirely,” Emma replied, forcing herself to sound calm. “Everything you said then seemed to refer to someone different. I could almost swear you mentioned Mr. Frank Churchill by name. I'm certain we spoke about his helping you by protecting you from the gypsies.”

“Oh, Miss Woodhouse, how you forget things!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember the main points of what I said perfectly well. I told you I wasn't surprised by your feelings; considering what he had done for you, they were very natural. You agreed and spoke with great warmth about how grateful you were. You even described what you had felt when you saw him step forward to rescue you. I remember it very clearly.”

“Oh dear!” Harriet cried. “Now I understand what you mean. But I was thinking about something quite different. I didn't mean the gypsies, or Mr. Frank Churchill. No!” she added with rising feeling. “I was thinking of a far more precious moment: when Mr. Knightley came and asked me to dance after Mr. Elton refused, and there was nobody else in the room to be my partner. That was the kindness, the noble goodness and generosity I meant. That was the help that first made me realize how much better he was than everyone else in the world.”

“Good God!” cried Emma. “This has been a terribly unfortunate—a dreadful misunderstanding! What are we to do?”

“Then you wouldn't have encouraged me if you had understood? Still, at least I can't be worse off than I would have been if I'd meant the other gentleman. And now—it is possible—”

She stopped for a few moments. Emma could say nothing.

“I'm not surprised, Miss Woodhouse,” Harriet continued, “that you see a great difference between them, whether for me or for anyone. You must think one is five hundred million times farther above me than the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that supposing—if—however strange it may seem—. You know you said yourself that more wonderful things had happened, that people with even greater differences in their positions had married than there would be between Mr. Frank Churchill and me. So it seems that even something like this might have happened before. And if I should be so fortunate that I can hardly express it—if Mr. Knightley should really—if he doesn't mind the difference between us, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, you won't oppose it or try to put obstacles in our way.
